analysis.one_liner: Bans landlord discrimination against housing voucher holders and rewards landlords who maintain their units.
analysis.headline: The Landlord Accountability Act was referred to three House committees in February 2022 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Housing Act to make it illegal to refuse to rent to someone because they use a Section 8 housing voucher. It would fine landlords up to $100,000 for deliberately letting a unit fall into disrepair so it no longer qualifies for federal housing assistance, and let tenants sue for $50,000 plus actual damages. It would also require HUD to answer and publish tenant complaints, give landlords a tax credit for maintenance costs if they fix complaints within 30 days, and fund local programs that help tenants fight landlord harassment.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly millions of families who rent with Section 8 vouchers, who in most states can legally be turned away by landlords simply for using the voucher. Also tenants in larger HUD-assisted buildings, who would get a staffed complaint line, a formal complaint process, and a public record of every complaint filed against their building. Voucher-accepting landlords who keep their units in good repair would get a tax credit covering their maintenance expenses, up to $500,000 a year.

how_it_helps.text: Adds voucher holders as a protected class under the Fair Housing Act, so refusing to rent to someone because they pay with a Section 8 voucher becomes illegal discrimination.

Makes it a violation, with a $100,000 civil penalty per action, for a landlord to deliberately fail to maintain a unit so it no longer qualifies for HUD assistance; tenants harmed can sue for $50,000 per violation plus their actual costs, including the cost of finding a new place.

Requires HUD to staff up its multifamily housing complaint line so tenants are not left on hold, run a formal complaint resolution program, and publish every complaint online with its disposition; landlords would also have to post tenants' rights notices and hotline numbers on every floor.

Gives qualifying landlords a tax credit equal to their maintenance expenses (capped at $2,500 per low-income unit, $100,000 per project, and $500,000 per owner) — but only if they fixed any HUD complaints within 30 days or received none.

Authorizes $25 million a year from 2023 through 2027 in grants to states, tribes, local governments, and nonprofits for tenant harassment prevention programs, including legal help for tenants facing illegal pressure to move out.
Provides that vouchers cannot legally be a reason to decline a tenant, which matters because most states place no such restriction on landlords.

analysis.who_pays: Landlords — especially owners of larger buildings with voucher tenants — would bear the cost of nondiscrimination compliance, mandated postings, penalties for deliberately disqualifying units, and public disclosure of complaints; a maintenance tax credit partially offsets this for landlords who fix problems promptly. Federal taxpayers would cover the tax credit's cost and the $25 million a year in grant money.
analysis.who_pays_short: Landlords, plus federal taxpayers for credits and grants

drawbacks.text: The maintenance tax credit is a new open-ended federal cost: every dollar a qualifying landlord spends on maintenance is creditable, up to $500,000 per owner per year, through 2032, so the total price to taxpayers depends entirely on how many landlords claim it.

The $100,000-per-violation penalty and $50,000 tenant damages could lead some landlords to leave the voucher program altogether rather than accept voucher tenants, which would shrink the very rental stock the bill's beneficiaries rely on.
The complaint resolution program is funded by redirecting administrative fees that otherwise support the day-to-day operation of the voucher program itself.
A landlord with no complaints gets the full tax credit even if its units are poorly maintained — complaints are the trigger, not inspection of conditions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For voucher holders, the protections are substantial and directly aimed at two of their most common problems: being refused outright and living in units that decay until they lose federal eligibility. The tax credit is a real concession to landlords and a real cost to taxpayers, but it is tied to actually fixing complaints, which gives it some accountability. The main honest risk is that harsh penalties could push marginal landlords out of the voucher program instead of into compliance. On balance the bill helps a vulnerable group at a moderate, partly offset cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee from the day it was introduced until Congress ended — referred to three House committees, then to a single Judiciary subcommittee, and never scheduled for a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Nydia Velazquez introduced the Landlord Accountability Act of 2022 on February 1, 2022, and it was referred the same day to the Financial Services Committee and additionally to Ways and Means and Judiciary.
The bill gained one cosponsor, a House Democrat, and no Republican support.
On November 1, 2022 — nine months after introduction — it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, which took no action.
No hearing, markup, or vote of any kind was scheduled in any of the three committees before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died without ever coming to the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords who decline voucher tenants or let federally assisted units decay to disqualify them are better off, since the bill's penalties, disclosure requirements, and nondiscrimination rule never took effect; taxpayers also avoided the cost of the new tax credit and grant program. Voucher holders gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Nydia Velazquez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 1, 2022 and championed protections for voucher holders, penalties for landlords who disqualify units, and a maintenance tax credit.

for.name: 1 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only additional support it attracted.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral; chaired by a Democrat in the 117th Congress
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — over the nine months before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill's tax credit provisions after referral.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Additional committee of referral (Fair Housing Act amendments)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties on November 1, 2022, where it died without action.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the bill's single cosponsor were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; no vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.industry: Residential landlords, especially owners of multifamily buildings with voucher tenants
industries.note: The bill would impose nondiscrimination rules, mandatory tenant-rights postings, public disclosure of complaints, and $100,000 penalties for deliberately letting units decay to lose HUD eligibility — but it pairs those burdens with a tax credit covering maintenance costs (up to $500,000 per owner per year) for landlords who fix complaints within 30 days. The industry's core interest in the bill ran against voucher holders: refusing to rent to voucher tenants is a way to keep the public rent subsidy out of a building, and that practice is what the bill would have ended.

industries.industry: Legal aid and nonprofit tenant-housing organizations
industries.note: The bill authorized $25 million a year for tenant harassment prevention programs, including legal assistance and counseling for tenants facing illegal pressure to vacate — services these organizations would deliver and would benefit from.
